units.title: Plant Systems
units.intro:
**Growth** = irreversible increase in size; **development** = new organs (leaf, flower). Seeds may stay dormant until water, warmth and oxygen arrive.

**Plant hormones:** auxin (tip → elongate cells, phototropism), gibberellin (stem / germination), cytokinin (cell division), ethene (ripening), abscisic acid (dormancy / stomatal close in drought).

cards.title: 6.1.1 Growth and Development in Flowering Plants
body: In plants growing points are found at the tip of stems and roots.
In special circumstances the young (immature) cells of a root, stem or leaf may become active and divide to form a new root or a new shoot.
Leaves have limited growth which determines their size and shape.
Young cells in the leaf-bud divide repeatedly to give rise to the leaf tissue.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Seed Dormancy and Germination
body: Dormant seeds are seeds which remain viable (alive) though metabolically inactive and incapable of germination under the conditions normally favourable for the species.
In other words, the seed is “asleep”, waiting for the ideal conditions to awaken.
**Seed dormancy** is a mechanism that ensures the survival of the species.
Dormancy enables the plant to avoid periods of environmental stress such as dry season or cold winter temperatures.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Plant growth hormones — chemical messengers of plants
body: **Step 1 — what they are.** Plant hormones are **chemical substances** that affect a plant’s ability to **respond to its environment**. They are usually **made in one part** of the plant and **transported to another** where they act — just like animal hormones, but plants have no glands; growing tips, young leaves, seeds and fruits make them.
**Step 2 — why “growth regulators”.** They can **stimulate or inhibit** growth, so they are also called **plant growth regulators**.
**Step 3 — they act on targets.** They interact with specific **target tissues** to cause responses such as **growth, flowering, fruit ripening, leaf fall or dormancy**.
**Step 4 — teamwork.** Each response is often the result of **two or more hormones acting together** — sometimes helping each other, sometimes opposing (antagonism).

**Step 5 — the five groups:** **auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid (ABA).** The first three mostly **promote** growth; ABA mostly **inhibits**; ethylene **ripens** fruit and speeds leaf fall.

cards.title: Auxins — the elongation and bending hormone
body: **The natural auxin** is **indoleacetic acid (IAA)**, produced in the **apical meristem of the shoot**, in actively growing shoot tips and in developing fruits.
**Main job — cell elongation.** IAA makes cells just behind the tip **stretch**, so the shoot grows longer.
**Phototropism (bending to light):** when light comes from one side, auxin collects on the **shaded side**; cells there elongate **more**, so the shoot **curves towards the light**.
**Geotropism:** auxin also redistributes under gravity, helping shoots grow up and roots grow down.

**Apical dominance:** auxin from the terminal bud **inhibits the lateral (side) buds**, so an intact plant grows tall with few branches. Remove the tip and the side buds grow — the plant becomes **bushy**.
**Other effects:** inhibits **abscission** (leaf/fruit fall), promotes **fruit development**, stimulates **root initiation**, and helps **cell division** and growth.

steps.text: **The tip makes auxin**, which moves down the shoot.
**Light from one side** → auxin moves to the **shaded side**.
**Shaded-side cells elongate more** → the shoot bends towards the light.

cards.title: Apical dominance — why pruning makes a plant bushy

steps.text: **Intact plant:** auxin from the terminal bud flows down and holds back the lateral buds → tall, few branches.
**Tip removed (pruned):** no auxin from the top → lateral buds grow → bushy plant. Gardeners “pinch out” tips of hedges, tea and tomato plants for this reason.

cards.title: Synthetic auxins — chemistry on the farm
body: **What:** cheap compounds made by chemists with structures **similar to IAA**.
**NAA (naphthalene acetic acid):** used to **promote root formation** in stem and leaf cuttings (rooting powder) — useful for propagating roses, coffee, grapevines.
**Fruit set:** gardeners spray auxins on **tomato** plants to **increase the number of fruits** on each plant.

**2,4-D — a selective herbicide (weed killer):** it **kills dicots** (broad-leaved weeds such as dandelion and pigweed) **without injuring monocots** (lawn grasses and cereals such as wheat, barley, maize, sorghum and teff). The dicot weeds grow so fast and abnormally that they die.

cards.title: Gibberellins — the “grow taller” hormone
body: **Main effect:** **stimulate the elongation of stems.** Spraying a plant with gibberellins usually makes it grow **taller than normal**. (Dwarf varieties often make little gibberellin.)

**Other effects:** stimulate **lateral buds**, **seed germination** (they switch on enzymes that digest the seed’s food store), **fruit development**, cell division and elongation; they **inhibit root initiation** (the opposite of auxin).
**Use:** sprayed on **grapes** to **increase fruit size** and the **distance between fruits** (less crowding, less rot).

cards.title: Cytokinins — the cell-division hormone
body: **Main effect:** **promote cell division** (cyto = cell, kinesis = division).
**Other effects:** stimulate **lateral buds**, **seed germination** and **cell elongation**; (they also delay ageing of leaves — extra).
**Tissue culture:** cytokinins are very important when plant tissue is grown in the laboratory. The **ratio of auxin to cytokinin** in the medium decides what the tissue makes.

cards.title: Abscisic acid (ABA) and ethylene — the “stop” and “ripen” hormones
body: **ABA generally inhibits other hormones**, such as the auxin IAA. It was first thought to cause **abscission** (leaf fall) — hence its name — but botanists now know that **ethylene is the main abscission hormone**.

**ABA and dormancy:** ABA brings about **dormancy in buds** (e.g. before a dry season) and **maintains dormancy in seeds**, so they do not germinate at the wrong time. (In drought it also closes stomata to save water.)
**Ethylene** is responsible for **fruit ripening** — softening, sweetening (starch → sugar) and colour change. With ABA it speeds the **abscission** of leaves and fruits.
**The odd one out:** unlike the other four, **ethylene is a gas** at room temperature, so it spreads through the air from one fruit to another — “one ripe fruit ripens the basket”.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (6.1.3)
body: **Abscisic acid is NOT the main abscission hormone** — ethylene is. ABA = dormancy/inhibition.
**Ethylene is the only gas.**
**Auxin inhibits lateral buds; cytokinin stimulates them.**
**Root initiation:** auxin promotes, gibberellin inhibits.
**Tissue culture:** high auxin → roots; low auxin (high cytokinin) → shoots.
**2,4-D kills dicots** (broad leaves), not monocots (grasses, cereals).

cards.title: Activity 6.3 — guavas and a ripe banana
cards.problem: Unripe guavas were sealed in bags alone (bags 1–4) or with a ripe banana (bags 5–8). After 2–3 days the cut guavas were tested with iodine. Describe the expected observations and explain them.

steps.text: Step 1: Identify the variable — the only difference is the **ripe banana**; bags 1–4 are the control.
Step 2: Observation — guavas with a banana turn **yellow, soften and smell sweet sooner**; control guavas stay greener and harder.
Step 3: Iodine test — control guavas stain **blue-black strongly** (much starch); test guavas stain **less** (starch has changed to sugar).
Step 4: Explanation — the ripe banana gives off **ethylene gas**; in a sealed bag it builds up and **speeds ripening** of the guava, which converts starch to sugars.
Step 5: Conclusion — ethylene is a gaseous hormone that ripens fruit; this is why one ripe fruit can ripen others nearby.

cards.answer: Guavas with a banana ripen faster and show less starch (weaker blue-black) because the banana releases ethylene gas, which promotes ripening.

cards.title: Apply it — weeds in a wheat field
cards.problem: A farmer near Mendefera sprays 2,4-D on a wheat field full of broad-leaved weeds. Predict and explain the result.

steps.text: Step 1: Wheat is a **monocot**; broad-leaved weeds are **dicots**.
Step 2: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin that is **selective** — it kills dicots but not monocots.
Step 3: The weeds grow abnormally and die; the wheat is unharmed and gets more water, light and minerals.

cards.answer: The broad-leaved (dicot) weeds die while the wheat (monocot) survives, so the crop yield increases.

cards.title: Apply it — making a bushy hedge
cards.problem: A gardener wants a thick, bushy hedge. What should she do, and which hormone explains it?

steps.text: Step 1: The terminal bud makes **auxin**, which suppresses lateral buds (apical dominance).
Step 2: Cutting off the shoot tips removes this auxin source.
Step 3: Lateral buds now grow into side branches → bushy hedge.

cards.answer: Trim (pinch out) the shoot tips regularly; removing the auxin source ends apical dominance so side branches grow.

cards.title: Apply it — tissue culture
cards.problem: In a tissue-culture lab, a piece of potato tissue produced many roots but no shoots. How should the medium be changed to get shoots?

steps.text: Step 1: Many roots → the medium has a **high auxin : cytokinin ratio**.
Step 2: Shoots need a **low** ratio.
Step 3: So reduce auxin and/or add more cytokinin.

cards.answer: Lower the auxin-to-cytokinin ratio (more cytokinin, less auxin).

cards.title: Step by step: Plant tissues
body: **Step 1:** Meristematic tissue: small, dividing cells at root and shoot tips (apical meristems – growth in length) and in the cambium (lateral meristem – growth in thickness).

**Step 2:** Permanent simple tissues: parenchyma (thin-walled living cells for storage and photosynthesis), collenchyma (unevenly thickened living cells for flexible support in young stems) and sclerenchyma (dead cells with lignified walls for rigid support – fibres and stone cells).
**Step 3:** Complex tissues: xylem (vessels and tracheids – carry water and minerals up, dead, lignified) and phloem (sieve tubes and companion cells – carry sugars both ways, living).
**Step 4:** Dermal tissue: epidermis with a waxy cuticle, stomata and root hairs.
**Step 5:** These tissues form three tissue systems: dermal, vascular and ground.
**Example:** Why can a young sunflower stem bend in the wind without breaking? Collenchyma gives flexible support; later, as the stem thickens, sclerenchyma and xylem give rigid support.

cards.title: 6.3.1 Tap and Fibrous Root Systems
body: The two principal functions of roots are the absorption of water and minerals, and anchorage.
When the seed germinates, the radicle is usually the first structure to appear; it becomes the first root and is called the **primary root**.
In many plants (e.g. beet, radish and carrot), the primary root remains the principal root throughout the life of the plant.
The development of a fibrous root system (like that of barley or wheat) is different from that of a tap root system.

cards.title: 6.3.2 Root growth regions — four zones behind the root tip
body: **Step 1 — the big picture.** A young root grows in length only at its **tip**. A long section of the tip shows **four regions** (from the tip upwards): **root cap → region of cell division → region of elongation → region of maturation**.
**Step 2 — not walls, but a gradient.** The regions are **not strictly separate**: cells made in one region gradually develop into those of the next as the tip moves on.

**Step 3 — follow one cell.** A cell is made by division just behind the cap, then **stretches** in the elongation zone, then **specialises** (e.g. into a root-hair cell or a xylem vessel) in the maturation zone. So reading the zones from tip to top is like watching a cell’s life story.

cards.title: The root tip, region by region

steps.text: **Root cap** — cup of parenchyma cells protecting the delicate tip; outer cells are worn away by soil.
**Region of cell division** — meristem; small cube-shaped cells with large nuclei, few tiny vacuoles; makes all root tissues and new cap cells.
**Region of elongation** — cells take in lots of water and grow long; small vacuoles merge into one or two large ones (up to 90 % of the cell).
**Region of maturation (differentiation, root-hair zone)** — cells become permanent tissues; root hairs absorb most water and minerals.

cards.title: Root cap and region of cell division
body: **Root cap:** made of **parenchyma** cells forming an **inverted cup** over the tip of each root. Its outer part is **rough and uneven** because cells are constantly **worn away** as the root pushes through the soil. **Main function: protect the delicate root tip** (the meristem). (Extra: its cells make slimy mucilage that eases the way and they sense gravity.)

**Where new cap cells come from:** the textbook says the cap “arises from cells in the region of elongation”, but in the next paragraph it states correctly that the **growing point (region of cell division) gives rise to new root cap cells**. Use the second statement in exams: **the meristem replaces the worn cap cells**.

**Region of cell division:** the zone **next to the root cap**, made of **actively dividing meristematic cells** from which **all other root tissues** are formed. Cells are **cube-shaped**, with **fairly large nuclei** and **few, if any, small vacuoles** — typical of cells that spend their energy dividing.

cards.title: Region of elongation and region of maturation
body: **Region of elongation:** immediately behind the growing point. Cells become **longer and somewhat wider**, remain **undifferentiated**, and grow rapidly by **taking in large quantities of water**. The tiny vacuoles **merge into one or two large vacuoles** that may fill **90 % or more** of the cell. This zone **pushes the tip forward** through the soil.

**Why growth stops above it:** only the **root cap and apical meristem actually move** through the soil, so there is **no further increase in length above the region of elongation** — older parts are anchored.

**Region of maturation** (also **region of differentiation** or **root-hair zone**): cells **mature and differentiate** into the **permanent tissues** — epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem, phloem.

**Root hairs:** each is a **slender lateral projection of a single epidermal cell**. The **cuticle is very thin** here. Any epidermal cell can absorb, but root hairs give a **much larger surface**, so **most water and minerals enter through root hairs**. They are **short-lived**: they wither as the root grows and new ones form nearer the tip.

cards.title: Experiment — where does a root grow?
cards.problem: A germinating bean root is marked with ink lines 1 mm apart, starting at the tip. After 24 hours the spacing is measured. Predict and explain the result.

steps.text: Step 1: Lines on the cap stay close; the cap only moves forward.
Step 2: Lines about 2–5 mm behind the tip become **widely spaced** — this is the **region of elongation**, where cells stretch.
Step 3: Lines further back (maturation zone) stay **1 mm apart** — no more growth there.
Step 4: Conclusion: growth in length happens in a short zone just behind the tip.

cards.answer: Marks just behind the tip (elongation zone) spread apart most; marks further back do not move apart, showing growth happens only near the tip.

cards.title: Exercise 6.3 Q1, Q2 and Q4
cards.problem: (1) What are the regions of root development? (2) What is the function of the root cap? (4) Describe the region of cell maturation.

steps.text: Step 1 (Q1): Root cap, region of cell division, region of elongation, region of maturation.
Step 2 (Q2): The root cap protects the delicate root tip (meristem) as it pushes through the soil; its worn cells are replaced from the meristem.

Step 3 (Q4): In the maturation (root-hair) zone cells differentiate into permanent tissues; epidermal cells grow root hairs with a thin cuticle that absorb most water and minerals; the hairs are short-lived.

cards.answer: (1) Root cap, region of cell division, region of elongation, region of maturation. (2) It protects the delicate root tip as the root pushes through the soil. (4) Cells differentiate into permanent tissues; epidermal cells form short-lived root hairs with a thin cuticle that absorb most water and minerals.

cards.title: Apply it — transplanting seedlings
cards.problem: Why should seedlings be transplanted with a ball of soil round their roots?

steps.text: Step 1: Most water is absorbed by delicate **root hairs** near the tip.
Step 2: Pulling a seedling out bare tears off the root hairs.
Step 3: With few root hairs the plant cannot absorb enough water and wilts; keeping soil round the roots protects them.

cards.answer: To avoid damaging the root hairs, which absorb most of the water and minerals.

**Root hairs are in the maturation zone**, not at the very tip.
**A root hair is one cell**, not many.
**Vacuoles:** tiny in the division zone, huge in the elongation zone.

cards.title: 6.3.3 Internal Structure of the Root
body: In cross section, a root has an epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, and xylem and phloem.
**The cortex** is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.
The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis.
Inside the endodermis is a cylinder of parenchyma cells called the pericycle.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary function of Abscisic Acid (ABA) in plants during environmental stress?

options.A: To promote rapid stem elongation and leaf growth
options.B: To accelerate fruit ripening and flower opening
options.C: To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit
options.D: To stimulate cell division in lateral buds

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define ABA as a stress hormone**
$$ABA$$ is synthesized in plastids and acts as a key stress signaler.

**Step 2: Connect with water conservation**
Under drought stress, $$ABA$$ causes potassium ions to exit guard cells, closing stomata to prevent transpiration water loss, and maintains seed dormancy.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit**.

**Step 1: Identify root vascular layers**
Water absorbed by roots passes through the epidermis and cortex toward the vascular cylinder.

**Step 2: Identify the regulatory barrier**
The endodermis is the innermost cortical layer. Its cell walls contain suberin (the Casparian strip), which blocks apoplastic water flow, forcing water to pass through cell membranes to regulate mineral entry.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Endodermis**.

lessons.title: The Shoot: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: 6.4 The shoot — stem, leaves and flowers
body: **The shoot system** is everything above the ground: **stems, leaves and flowers**. The stem is the frame and pipeline, the leaves are the food factories, and the flowers are the reproductive organs.
**Order of this lesson:** 6.4.1 stem → 6.4.2 leaf → 6.4.3 flower, each with external structure, internal structure and functions.

cards.title: 6.4.1 The stem — functions and external structure
body: **Four functions of the stem:** (i) it **bears the leaves**; (ii) holds them where they get **plenty of light**; (iii) **conducts** water and minerals up to the leaves and manufactured food from the leaves to other parts; (iv) in some plants it **stores food** (e.g. potato tuber, sugar cane).
**What a stem is:** an **axis** with leaves attached and a **growing point at the tip**. The tip is protected by overlapping young leaves forming the **terminal bud**.
**Leaf arrangement:** **alternate** (one leaf per node, on alternate sides), **opposite** (two per node, facing each other) or **whorled** (three or more per node).
**Nodes and internodes:** a **node** is where a leaf attaches; the stretch between two nodes is the **internode**.

**Axil and axillary bud:** the angle between a leaf and the stem is the **axil**; the bud in it is the **axillary bud** (the textbook calls the angle itself the axillary bud). Axillary buds grow into **new branches or flowers**.

cards.title: Internal structure of a young dicot stem (sunflower)
body: A thin transverse section seen under the microscope shows **four regions, from outside to centre**:
**a. Epidermis** — **one cell thick**; outer walls thickened with **cutin**, forming a waterproof **cuticle** that stops water loss and keeps out gases and germs.
**b. Cortex** — just inside the epidermis, outside the conducting tissue; **parenchyma** cells with **large intercellular spaces** (for gas exchange and storage).

**c. Vascular bundles** — arranged in a **ring**. Each has **phloem** on the outside (carries **manufactured food** from leaves to other parts) and **xylem** on the inside (carries **water and minerals** from roots to leaves). Between them, **cambium** cells divide constantly to make **new phloem and xylem**, so the stem can grow thicker.
**d. Pith** — the **centre**; the **most extensive tissue**, of **parenchyma** with the **largest cells** in the section; stores food and water.

steps.text: **Dicot (sunflower):** bundles in a **ring**, cambium between xylem and phloem, cortex outside the ring, large pith in the centre.
**Monocot (maize):** bundles **scattered** throughout, **no cambium**, **no distinct pith**, very little cortex.

cards.title: Memory hook — outside to centre: “Every Cat Visits Paris”

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q1
cards.problem: List the pattern of tissues in a young dicot stem from the outside to the centre.

steps.text: Step 1: Outermost — epidermis (with cuticle).
Step 2: Then cortex (parenchyma).
Step 3: Then the ring of vascular bundles — phloem, cambium, xylem (outside → inside).
Step 4: Centre — pith.

cards.answer: Epidermis → cortex → vascular bundles (phloem, cambium, xylem) → pith.

cards.title: Apply it — ring-barking a tree
cards.problem: Goats strip a complete ring of bark from a young tree. The leaves stay green for weeks, but the tree later dies. Explain.

steps.text: Step 1: Bark includes the **phloem**, which lies outside the xylem.
Step 2: The xylem (inside) is untouched, so water still reaches the leaves — they stay green.
Step 3: Food made in the leaves cannot pass the ring through phloem to the roots.
Step 4: The roots starve, stop absorbing, and the whole tree dies.

cards.answer: Removing the ring removes the phloem: water still rises in the xylem, but food can no longer reach the roots, which die, and then the tree dies.

cards.title: Activity 6.8 — identify the slide
cards.problem: A slide of a stem section shows vascular bundles scattered all over, with no central pith. Is it a dicot or a monocot? Give two reasons.

steps.text: Step 1: Scattered bundles → monocot.
Step 2: No pith → monocot.
Step 3: Check for cambium — absent in monocots.

cards.answer: Monocot — scattered bundles, no pith (and no cambium).

cards.title: 6.4.2 The leaf — the food factory: external structure
body: **Job:** the leaf is the **site of food production**. Here the plant takes in **light energy** and **carbon dioxide** for photosynthesis and **releases oxygen**.
**Monocot vs dicot leaves:** monocots typically have **simple leaves with parallel venation**; dicots have **branching (net) venation** and many shapes.
**Three parts of a typical dicot leaf:**
**① Blade (lamina)** — the flat, extended part. Its edge is the **margin**: **toothed** in sunflower, **smooth** in bean. **Veins** run through it carrying water and nutrients.
**② Petiole** — the short stalk attaching the leaf to the stem; it continues into the centre of the lamina as the **midrib**.
**③ Leaf base** — the point of attachment. Some leaves have **stipules** (small scale-like or leaf-like outgrowths) at the base; in most monocots the base widens into a **sheath** around the stem.

cards.title: Internal structure of the leaf — layer by layer
body: **Upper epidermis:** a **single layer** of closely fitting, comparatively large, water-filled cells, covered by a **thick waxy cuticle** that reduces water loss. Cells are **transparent**, so light passes through.
**Palisade layer (upper mesophyll):** **2–3 layers** of **long, cylindrical** cells packed with **many chloroplasts** — the main photosynthetic tissue, placed where light is strongest.
**Spongy layer (lower mesophyll):** **loosely packed** cells in a network with **many air spaces**; they also contain chloroplasts. The air spaces let gases diffuse through the leaf.
**Veins (vascular bundles):** continuous with those of the stem — **xylem** brings water and minerals; **phloem** takes food away. They also support the blade.

**Lower epidermis:** a single layer of **small cells** with **very numerous stomata** between them. Each stoma is a pore between two guard cells. (In some plants stomata occur on both surfaces; in others only on the lower surface.)
**Stomata** control **water loss** and allow **free diffusion of CO₂ and O₂**.

cards.title: Gas exchange through the stomata — step by step (Activity 6.9)
body: **Step 1:** In light, photosynthesis uses CO₂, so CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls.
**Step 2:** CO₂ **diffuses in** through the open **stomata** (mostly on the lower surface) into the **air spaces** of the spongy layer.
**Step 3:** It moves through the air channels to the **palisade cells**, passes through the **wet cell walls** and **dissolves** in the cell sap, reaching the chloroplasts.
**Step 4:** **Oxygen** made by photosynthesis diffuses the opposite way and out through the stomata.
**Step 5:** Water vapour also escapes through open stomata (**transpiration**). Stomata **close at night** or in drought, saving water but stopping CO₂ entry.

cards.title: From glucose to starch
body: **Photosynthesis:** in sunlight, **water and carbon dioxide react inside the chloroplast** to form **glucose** (and oxygen). The flat, expanded leaf gives a **large surface area** — the best shape for absorbing light.

**Storage:** glucose is **removed from the cell sap quickly** and turned into **insoluble starch**, stored as small solid **starch grains** in the chloroplasts. Insoluble starch does not upset the water balance (osmosis) of the cell.

**Note on “leucoplasts”:** the textbook says starch is deposited “in the form of leucoplasts”. Leucoplasts are actually **colourless plastids that store starch in non-green parts** (e.g. potato tubers, roots); in the leaf itself, starch grains lie **inside the chloroplasts**.

cards.title: Explain — why most stomata are on the lower surface
cards.problem: Why do many plants have more stomata on the lower surface of the leaf?

steps.text: Step 1: The upper surface faces the sun and is hotter.
Step 2: Stomata there would lose much more water by evaporation.
Step 3: On the shaded, cooler lower surface water loss is less, while CO₂ can still enter the air spaces of the spongy layer just above.

cards.answer: To reduce water loss: the lower surface is cooler and shaded, yet still opens directly into the spongy air spaces.

cards.title: 6.4.3 The flower — structure
body: **What a flower is:** the part of the shoot **specially modified for reproduction**. It sits on a **flower stalk (pedicel)** whose swollen tip is the **receptacle**.

**Four whorls (rings) of floral parts**, from the **outside towards the centre**: **calyx (sepals) → corolla (petals) → androecium (stamens) → gynoecium (pistil/carpels)**. (The textbook lists gynoecium before androecium; in a real flower the **stamens form a ring outside the central pistil**.)
**Calyx:** the outermost whorl of **sepals** — modified leaves that **protect the flower in the bud**; usually green, sometimes brightly coloured.
**Corolla:** the **petals** — often brightly coloured and scented to **attract insects** (pollinators); they may be **joined into a tube** or **free**.
**Androecium (male):** the **stamens**. Each stamen = a **filament** (stalk) supporting an **anther** (sac containing **pollen grains**).

**Gynoecium (female):** one or more **pistils (carpels)**. Each pistil = **stigma** (flattened or branched top with a **sticky surface** that catches pollen) + **style** (stalk joining stigma to ovary) + **ovary** (enlarged base housing the **ovules**).

cards.title: Flower long section — the four whorls

steps.text: **Calyx — sepals:** protect the bud.
**Corolla — petals:** attract pollinators.
**Androecium — stamens** (filament + anther): make pollen.
**Gynoecium — pistil** (stigma + style + ovary): receives pollen; ovules inside.

cards.title: Describing flowers and plants — six terms
body: **Complete flower:** has all four parts (sepals, petals, stamens, pistil). **Incomplete:** one or more missing.
**Essential parts** are the **stamens and pistil** (they make the gametes).
**Perfect (bisexual) flower:** has **both** stamens and pistil (e.g. bean, hibiscus). **Imperfect (unisexual):** has **only one** of them.
**Monoecious plant** (“one house”): **separate male and female flowers on the same plant** — e.g. **maize** (tassel = male, cob = female), **pumpkin**.
**Dioecious plant** (“two houses”): **male and female flowers on different plants** — e.g. **papaya**; a farmer needs at least one male tree near the female trees to get fruit.

cards.title: Function of the flower — pollination
body: **Main function:** produce **male and female gametes** and bring them together. The **pollen grains** (which carry the male gametes) are made in the **anthers**; the **ovules** (which contain the egg) are made inside the **ovary**.
**Pollination** = the **transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma** of a flower of the **same kind (species)**.
**Self-pollination:** pollen goes to the stigma of the **same flower** or **another flower on the same plant**.

**Cross-pollination:** pollen goes to the stigma of a flower on **another plant** (of the same species) — carried by insects, wind, birds or water. It mixes genes from two parents, giving **more variation**.

cards.title: Fertilization and double fertilization — step by step
body: **Step 1 — germination of pollen.** Pollen landing on the stigma is nourished by a **sticky (sugary) substance** and **germinates**, growing a **pollen tube**.

**Step 2 — two nuclei become three.** A pollen grain has a **generative nucleus** and a **tube nucleus**. The generative nucleus divides into **two male nuclei**. The tube nucleus and the two male nuclei travel down the tube **within the style**.
**Step 3 — reaching the ovule.** The tube grows to the **ovary**, enters the **ovule through the micropyle**, and its tip **bursts**, releasing the two male nuclei.
**Step 4 — inside the ovule (embryo sac):** an **egg nucleus**, **two polar nuclei**, **three antipodal cells** and **two synergids**.
**Step 5 — fusion one:** one male nucleus + **egg nucleus** → **zygote** (grows into the embryo).
**Step 6 — fusion two:** the second male nucleus + the **two polar nuclei** → **endosperm** nucleus (grows into the food store of the seed).
**Step 7 — name it:** two fusions at once = **double fertilization**, found **only in flowering plants**.
**Step 8 — after fertilization:** petals, stamens and style **wither**; the **ovule becomes the seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**.

steps.text: **Pollen tube** grows down the style and enters the ovule through the micropyle, carrying two male nuclei.
**Male nucleus 1 + egg → zygote** (2n) → embryo.
**Male nucleus 2 + two polar nuclei → endosperm** (3n, extra detail) → food store.

cards.title: Memory hook — whorls outside → in: “Some People Sing Professionally”
body: Sepals, Petals, Stamens, Pistil — and remember **STAMEN has “MEN” = male**.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (6.4.3)
body: **Pollination ≠ fertilization.** Pollination moves pollen; fertilization fuses nuclei.
**Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.** Students often swap them.
**Double fertilization:** egg + male nucleus = zygote; two polar nuclei + male nucleus = endosperm.
**Monoecious = one plant has both kinds of flower**; dioecious = separate male and female plants.
**Stamens lie outside the pistil** in the flower.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q3 and Q4
cards.problem: (3) What are the components of the stamen and the pistil? (4) Which parts of the flower give rise to a seed and to a fruit?

steps.text: Step 1 (Q3): Stamen = filament + anther (with pollen).
Step 2 (Q3): Pistil = stigma + style + ovary (with ovules).
Step 3 (Q4): After double fertilization the ovule develops into the seed.
Step 4 (Q4): The ovary enlarges into the fruit.

cards.answer: Stamen: filament and anther. Pistil: stigma, style and ovary. Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q5
cards.problem: Distinguish: (a) self- and cross-pollination; (b) perfect and imperfect flowers; (c) monoecious and dioecious plants.

steps.text: Step 1 (a): Self — pollen to a stigma of the same flower or same plant; cross — to a flower on another plant of the same species.
Step 2 (b): Perfect — has both stamens and pistil; imperfect — has only one of them.
Step 3 (c): Monoecious — male and female flowers on the same plant (maize); dioecious — on different plants (papaya).

cards.answer: (a) Self: pollen to the same flower/plant; cross: to another plant of the same species. (b) Perfect: both stamens and pistil; imperfect: only one. (c) Monoecious: male and female flowers on one plant (maize); dioecious: on separate plants (papaya).

cards.title: Apply it — a lonely papaya tree
cards.problem: A farmer plants one papaya tree. It flowers every year but never bears fruit. Explain and advise.

steps.text: Step 1: Papaya is **dioecious** — male and female flowers are on different trees.
Step 2: If the tree is male it can never fruit; if female, it has no pollen source nearby.
Step 3: Without pollination there is no fertilization, so no ovary becomes a fruit.
Step 4: Advice — plant several trees, including at least one male, near the female trees.

cards.answer: Papaya is dioecious; the single tree cannot be pollinated (or is male). Plant male and female trees together.

body: Soil water is absorbed by the root hairs.

options.A: Two sperm cells fertilize two separate egg cells to produce fraternal twins.
options.B: One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.

**Step 1: Review angiosperm reproductive events**

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.**

questions.q: Describe double fertilization in flowering plants.

One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form the zygote, which becomes the embryo; the second fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm, the food store. questions.q: Distinguish between pollination and fertilization.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species. Fertilization is the fusion of a male nucleus with the egg nucleus (and, in flowering plants, another male nucleus with the polar nuclei) inside the ovule. Pollination comes first.

questions.q: Why do insect-pollinated flowers usually have large, brightly coloured, scented petals?
questions.answer: The petals (corolla) attract insect pollinators by their colour and scent. Insects visiting for nectar pick up pollen from the anthers and carry it to the stigma of another flower, bringing about (cross-)pollination.
